doc.title: Eddie Marshall interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

chapter: Family and early playing in Springfield
title: Piano lessons and drums in his father's dance band
summary: Piano from 10 to 14, learning drums at his father's rehearsals, and at 14 replacing the drummer at Westover Air Force Base gigs.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Okay. But did you ever play with your father?

Oh yeah. Oh boy. I mean that’s how I started playing music. I started playing, I always took piano lessons. Like if you have a dad and mom and aunts, it’s either guitar or piano, and back in those days you were like really country if you played the guitar. If you were a black kid playing guitar, forget it. I didn’t want that image, I was too cool for that. I didn’t want to play the piano either but there was nothing I could do. So like from 10 to 14, that’s what I did, I took piano lessons. And I really enjoyed it. It was classical piano. But my dad always had rehearsals at the house, from the time I can remember. And of course when the drummer got off the drums I would jump on there. Even though I was six years — then they’d throw me off. But I kept on, I was just fascinated, during the rehearsals, I never even thought about it after rehearsal, but while we were there, I don’t know if I was trying to get my dad’s attention, but by the time I was 14, I could actually play the beats that they played. It was like a dance band. And they worked at the Westover Air Force Base and stuff like that and wore suits and all this. So there was one time, the drummer, Tommy, Tommy Johnson I believe his name was, he had trouble with his alimony payments. And they got a call the police were going to come and get him.

Anyhow he split and left the drums there. And then my dad was stuck. So I said, “Hey dad, you know, I know all these songs.” I was 14 and I was still in junior high school. And I was at an Air Force base with my dad and so I started doing these gigs at the Air Force base with my music teacher, because there was a young music teacher in the schools in Massachusetts during those days, the forties and fifties, you had a music teacher. And this guy played the trumpet in my dad’s band. So it was like a real secret that this 14-year-old kid’s playing in the band. And that’s how I started off. And I kept my day job, I kept my paper route.
Don’t quit your day gig yet.
Don’t know how this is going to go.
